title: Platform Reliability, Chaos Engineering & Kubernetes High-Availability Primitives
summary: Master cloud-native platform resilience: executing automated chaos experiments (pod kills, network latency) with Chaos Mesh, enforcing voluntary disruption protection via PodDisruptionBudgets (PDB), protecting critical system daemons with PriorityClasses, and implementing graceful zero-downtime container lifecycle termination using preStop hooks.
learningObjectives: Configure PodDisruptionBudgets (PDB) to safeguard microservice quorum during voluntary node drains and cluster upgrades.
Implement PriorityClasses with preemption policies to guarantee critical system workloads schedule over batch jobs.
Execute chaos injection experiments in the terminal and verify graceful shutdown using container preStop lifecycle hooks.

curriculumModules.title: High-Availability Primitives: PodDisruptionBudgets & PriorityClasses
curriculumModules.conceptSummary: PodDisruptionBudgets (PDB) declare the minimum percentage or number of replicas that must remain running during voluntary disruptions (e.g. node drains, auto-scaling down). PriorityClasses assign integer scheduling priorities (e.g. 1000000 for critical tiers) and preemption policies (PreemptLowerPriority), ensuring vital services evict lower-priority batch workloads when cluster capacity is saturated.
curriculumModules.productionArchitecturePattern: Mandate minAvailable: 2 or maxUnavailable: 1 PDBs across all production Deployments with >= 3 replicas, and assign high-priority PriorityClasses to ingress, DNS, and control-plane controllers.

curriculumModules.title: Chaos Engineering & Graceful Pod Termination with preStop Hooks
curriculumModules.conceptSummary: Chaos engineering proves system resilience by proactively injecting synthetic failures (pod crashes, packet loss, DNS corruption). When pods terminate, Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, but endpoint deregistration and kube-proxy iptables propagation can take several seconds. A container lifecycle preStop hook (e.g. sleep 15) keeps the container running briefly to drain active connections without dropping requests.
curriculumModules.productionArchitecturePattern: Always add a preStop sleep hook (sleep 10-15s) paired with an extended terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30-45s) on HTTP services behind Ingress / Service meshes to guarantee zero 502/504 connection resets during rolling deployments.

labs.title: Configuring PodDisruptionBudgets & Critical PriorityClasses
labs.scenario: Safeguard payment processing from voluntary eviction: author and apply a cluster-scoped PriorityClass named production-critical with value 1000000 and preemptionPolicy PreemptLowerPriority. Next, author and apply a PodDisruptionBudget named payment-pdb in namespace production targeting selector app: payment-api with minAvailable: 2.
labs.productionContext: PDBs guarantee that routine node upgrades or automated cluster autoscaler downscaling events never drop service replicas below high-availability quorum.
objectives: Apply PodDisruptionBudget payment-pdb in namespace production with minAvailable: 2.
labs.starterManifest:
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: production-critical
value: 1000000
globalDefault: false
preemptionPolicy: PreemptLowerPriority
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: payment-pdb
  namespace: production
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: payment-api

steps.instruction: Save and apply PriorityClass and PDB manifests to cluster.

validationRules.name: payment-pdb
validationRules.remediation: Apply PodDisruptionBudget payment-pdb in namespace production

troubleshootingGuide.problem: PriorityClass or PodDisruptionBudget missing or minAvailable incorrect.
troubleshootingGuide.cause: PriorityClass is cluster-scoped; PDB must be in production namespace.
troubleshootingGuide.solution: Verify /reliability/ha-primitives.yaml has correct YAML structure and re-apply.

labs.title: Injecting Chaos Experiments & Validating Graceful preStop Hooks
labs.scenario: Validate rolling deployment resilience under chaos: author a Pod manifest in /reliability/graceful-api.yaml in namespace production with a container lifecycle preStop hook executing ['/bin/sh', '-c', 'sleep 15'] and terminationGracePeriodSeconds set to 30. Apply to namespace production, then run chaos experiment pod-kill -n production to test self-healing.
labs.productionContext: Container preStop sleep hooks allow in-flight HTTP connections to complete and load balancers to deregister endpoints before the container receives SIGKILL.
objectives: Deploy Pod graceful-api in namespace production with preStop hook.
Execute chaos experiment pod-kill in namespace production.
labs.starterManifest:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: graceful-api
  namespace: production
  labels:
    app: graceful-api
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: nginx:1.27-alpine
      lifecycle:
        preStop:
          exec:
            command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 15"]

steps.title: Author Pod manifest with lifecycle preStop hook
Apply Pod to production namespace
steps.instruction: Apply the Pod to namespace production.

steps.title: Execute chaos experiment
steps.instruction: Run chaos experiment pod-kill in namespace production.

validationRules.description: Pod graceful-api exists in namespace production
validationRules.name: graceful-api
validationRules.remediation: Deploy Pod graceful-api in namespace production

solutionCommands:
cat << 'EOF' > /reliability/graceful-api.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: graceful-api
  namespace: production
  labels:
    app: graceful-api
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
  containers:
    - name: api

      lifecycle:
        preStop:
          exec:
            command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 15"]
EOF

troubleshootingGuide.cause: Pod was not created in production namespace or chaos experiment was omitted.
troubleshootingGuide.solution: Apply /reliability/graceful-api.yaml to production and execute chaos experiment pod-kill -n production.

assessmentQuestions.question: What is the difference between a voluntary disruption and an involuntary disruption in Kubernetes, and which one does a PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) protect against?
options: PDBs only protect against involuntary hardware power outages.

Voluntary disruptions are initiated by users or cluster operators (node drains, cluster upgrades, autoscaler scale-down), and PDBs strictly enforce availability limits during these events; involuntary disruptions are unpreventable hardware/kernel crashes.
Voluntary disruptions happen when containers run out of memory.
PDBs are used only for batch cronjobs.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: PodDisruptionBudgets govern voluntary administrative disruptions (kubectl drain, cluster upgrade, cluster autoscaling) to ensure a quorum of pods remains active. Involuntary disruptions (hardware failures, kernel panics) cannot be prevented by PDBs.

assessmentQuestions.question: Why should web microservices configure a container lifecycle preStop hook with a brief sleep (e.g. sleep 15) when running in production Kubernetes?
options: To cool down the physical CPU before shutting down the pod.

When a Pod enters Terminating, endpoint removal and iptables/IPVS rule updates propagate asynchronously across nodes; a preStop sleep delays sending SIGTERM to the process, allowing in-flight requests to complete while new traffic is routed away.
To force the container to dump its memory heap to disk.
Kubernetes requires all pods to sleep for 15 seconds before rebooting.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: Endpoint deregistration takes a few seconds to propagate through the API server, endpoint controller, and kube-proxy. A preStop hook sleep ensures the container keeps servicing requests until it is removed from all load balancing pools, eliminating 502 Bad Gateway errors.
